item.text:
1. **Section 2, chapeau — undefined “Secretary.”** The bill repeatedly assigns determinations to “the Secretary” without specifying the Secretary of Commerce or another official, creating uncertainty about who administers the Act and whether any purported determination is valid.

2. **Section 2 — undefined “artificial intelligence model” and “artificial intelligence system.”** The Act never defines either term or explains their relationship. Companies could argue that a particular agent, model ensemble, hybrid human-machine operation, or continuously updated service is neither—or is not the same “system” that was trained.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — arbitrary boundary at exactly \(10^{26}\) operations.** The provision covers only training using “greater than” \(10^{26}\) operations, so a run using exactly that amount is not covered. More importantly, a fixed threshold will become obsolete as algorithms and hardware improve.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — “single training run” invites division of training.** A developer could split training among successive runs, checkpoints, subsidiaries, sites, or separately trained components, keeping each nominal “run” below the threshold while producing an equivalently capable system.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — no aggregation of pretraining and subsequent work.** The text does not say whether fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, post-training, synthetic-data generation, architecture search, or repeated failed runs count toward training compute. A company could assign the relevant capability gains to supposedly separate post-training activities.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — no treatment of distributed or federated training.** The bill does not expressly aggregate computations conducted simultaneously across machines, facilities, corporate affiliates, or countries. Developers could characterize each distributed component as a separate run.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — compute measurement is underspecified.** “Integer or floating-point operations” does not specify precision, sparsity, skipped operations, mixed-precision arithmetic, estimated versus actual operations, or how specialized accelerators are counted. This makes the threshold contestable and potentially favors architectures whose work is difficult to express as conventional operations.

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — coverage depends on hard-to-prove historical facts.** Enforcement would require the government to establish how much compute a training run actually used, but the Act imposes no recordkeeping, metering, audit, or telemetry requirement on model developers or most facilities.

9. **Section 2(1)(A) — capability-independent safe harbor below the threshold.** An extremely capable system is lawful unless it crosses the compute threshold or the Secretary separately makes a determination under subparagraph (B). Algorithmic improvements, model compression, distillation, transfer learning, or theft of weights could therefore evade automatic coverage.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — coverage exists only after a discretionary determination.** A system that plainly exceeds human performance is not covered under this prong until the Secretary “determines” that it does. A developer may remain free to train and deploy it during agency delay, litigation, or deliberate nonaction.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — vague capability standard.** “Substantially exceeding,” “human performance,” “most,” and “cognitive tasks” lack benchmarks, reference populations, weighting rules, and testing methods. The vagueness creates both evasion opportunities and due-process problems, especially because criminal penalties attach.

12. **Section 2(1)(B) — “most cognitive tasks” may exclude dangerously superhuman systems.** A system could be overwhelmingly capable in strategically important domains—AI research, cyber operations, persuasion, weapons design, or biotechnology—without exceeding humans across a numerical majority of all conceivable cognitive tasks.

13. **Section 2(1)(B) — no procedure for determinations.** The bill supplies no testing authority, evidentiary standard, notice procedure, effective date, emergency process, appeal mechanism, or rule for confidential evidence. That omission will slow determinations and invite Administrative Procedure Act and due-process challenges.

14. **Section 2(1)(B) — possible retroactivity and fair-notice problem.** The text does not say whether a determination applies only prospectively or renders earlier conduct unlawful. Applying it backward would be especially vulnerable in criminal cases; applying it only forward leaves earlier deployment untouched.

15. **Section 2(1) — no anti-circumvention or successor-system rule.** A covered model could be distilled, quantized, copied, renamed, fine-tuned, divided into modules, or incorporated into a new product claimed to be a different system. The bill does not specify when derivatives, ensembles, wrappers, or substantially similar weights remain covered.

16. **Section 2(2) — “U.S. person” omits many U.S.-connected actors.** It includes citizens and state-law corporations but not expressly permanent residents, persons domiciled in the United States, partnerships, LLCs, trusts, associations, nonprofits, federally or territorially chartered entities, or other legal persons.

17. **Section 2(2) — easy foreign-entity workaround.** A U.S. company could move prohibited work into a separately incorporated foreign affiliate, joint venture, contractor, or foundation. The Act has no ownership, control, beneficial-ownership, direction, facilitation, conspiracy, or aiding-and-abetting rule that clearly reaches the U.S. parent and its personnel.

18. **Section 2(2) — foreign subsidiaries of U.S. corporations are not clearly covered.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary is not itself a “U.S. person,” even if wholly owned and controlled from the United States. Section 3 does not expressly prohibit a U.S. parent from financing, directing, licensing technology to, or benefiting from that subsidiary’s work.

19. **Section 2(3) — undefined “data center” and “operator.”** The bill provides no rule for identifying a facility’s boundaries or determining who operates it when the owner, landlord, cloud provider, chip owner, and customer are different entities. Companies could divide one campus into nominally separate data centers or dispute which party had the registration duty.

20. **Section 2(3) — undefined “advanced AI chips.”** No technical threshold, product list, performance measure, or updating mechanism identifies a qualifying chip. Commodity accelerators, custom ASICs, neuromorphic devices, foreign chips, or future hardware could fall outside the term or generate prolonged litigation.

21. **Section 2(3) — facility threshold is readily avoidable.** A facility with exactly 50,000 chips is excluded, and workloads can be distributed among multiple sub-threshold sites. The definition does not aggregate colocated facilities, commonly controlled facilities, interconnected clusters, or leased capacity.

22. **Section 2(3) — chip count is a poor and static proxy.** Chips vary enormously in capability, and future chips may make dangerous training possible with far fewer than 50,001 units. The Act provides no authority to update the threshold or substitute a performance- or compute-based measure.

23. **Section 3(a) — undefined operative verbs.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” have no statutory meanings or boundary rules. Routine research, fine-tuning, copying weights, hosting an API, internal use, publication, maintenance, and operation of an autonomous agent could all be disputed.

24. **Section 3(a) — important enabling conduct is not expressly prohibited.** The bill does not clearly ban financing, acquiring, possessing, transferring, exporting, importing, selling, licensing, hosting, providing compute for, publishing weights for, or materially assisting a covered system. Companies could facilitate foreign development without themselves “training, developing, or deploying” the system.

25. **Section 3(a) — territorial language is uncertain for organizations and remote conduct.** “Any person in the United States” is unclear when an overseas entity acts through U.S. servers, employees, cloud regions, or contractors, or when a person in the United States remotely directs foreign machines. The ambiguity will complicate jurisdiction and venue.

26. **Section 3(a) — no rule for joint, indirect, or attempted conduct.** The provision does not expressly cover attempts, conspiracies, substantial steps, causation through another person, or knowing assistance. Ordinary background doctrines may not reach every civil violation and are an uncertain substitute for explicit anti-evasion language.

27. **Section 3(b) — grandfather clause exempts systems indefinitely.** Any system whose “training began” before enactment is exempt from the entire prohibition, with no limit on later compute, capability, fine-tuning, deployment, replication, or commercialization. A developer could begin token training before enactment and claim that all later work belongs to the grandfathered system.

28. **Section 3(b) — “training began” is undefined and easily manufactured.** The Act does not require a minimum amount of bona fide training or identify when a new run, architecture, dataset, checkpoint, or successor becomes a new system. Companies could commence placeholder runs for many anticipated models before enactment.

29. **Section 3(b) — exemption is broader than necessary to avoid retroactivity.** It says subsection (a) “shall not apply to a covered AI system,” rather than merely allowing already completed training. Thus it appears to immunize future development and deployment, not just pre-enactment conduct.

30. **Section 3(c) — unlimited “safety evaluation” loophole.** Any otherwise prohibited activity can be characterized as conducted “for the purpose” of safety evaluation, without authorization, necessity, proportionality, containment, independent oversight, or a prohibition on commercial use. Mixed-purpose projects could invoke safety as one purpose while continuing capability development.

31. **Section 3(c) — subjective-purpose test impedes enforcement.** Liability may turn on asserted intent rather than objective conduct, allowing defendants to create internal documentation labeling work as safety evaluation. The bill does not assign the burden of proof or require advance approval.

32. **Section 3(c) — exemption permits deployment.** Because it exempts “activities” from all of subsection (a), it could authorize real-world deployment of a covered system whenever deployment is described as an evaluation. There are no limits on users, scale, duration, access, or dangerous capabilities.

33. **Section 4(a) — no registration deadline or required information.** Operators are told to register, but not when, how, or with what identifying, ownership, hardware, customer, or capacity information. The Department also receives no express rulemaking authority to fill these gaps.

34. **Section 4 — registry covers only very large facilities.** Training at smaller domestic facilities, distributed clusters, foreign facilities, or through aggregated cloud capacity triggers no registration obligation. Developers themselves have no registration requirement even when approaching the compute threshold.

35. **Section 4(b) — workload reports are too vague.** “Describing the computing workloads” does not require customer identities, compute totals, model architecture, training purpose, chip utilization, run aggregation, or notification before a dangerous run begins. Quarterly reporting may reveal a prohibited training run only months after completion.

36. **Section 4(b) — certification has no specified standard.** The text does not say who must certify, whether certification must be under penalty of perjury, or whether it attests to accuracy after reasonable inquiry. “Certified by the operator” therefore adds little accountability.

37. **Section 4 — no monitoring, audit, inspection, subpoena, or record-retention authority.** Commerce is not expressly empowered to verify reports, inspect facilities, require chip telemetry, compel records, or preserve logs. Self-reporting entities can conceal or mischaracterize workloads with little prospect of detection.

38. **Sections 4 and 5 — no penalty for registry violations.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3. Failure to register, file reports, report accurately, or retain supporting information therefore carries no express civil or criminal penalty.

39. **Section 5 — no enforcement authority or mechanism.** The Act does not identify an enforcing agency, authorize administrative orders or civil actions, assign jurisdiction, specify venue, or state who may seek penalties. It also lacks express authority for injunctions, emergency shutdowns, seizure, forfeiture, impoundment of chips, or deletion and containment of model weights.

40. **Section 5(a) — penalty may be economically inadequate.** A maximum of $1 million per day may be trivial compared with the value of frontier-model development and does not scale with revenue, compute expenditure, harm, or number of systems. There is no mandatory minimum, disgorgement, restitution, or recovery of profits.

41. **Section 5(a) — “each day” is ill-suited to instantaneous conduct.** Copying, transferring, releasing, or briefly deploying a model may occur in less than a day, and the text does not define when a violation begins or ends. It is also unclear whether simultaneous prohibited activities, systems, facilities, or responsible parties generate separate penalties.

42. **Section 5(a) — no penalty factors or limitations rules.** The statute supplies no factors for selecting a penalty up to the maximum and no express statute of limitations or tolling rule for concealed violations. This can produce inconsistent enforcement and unnecessary litigation.

43. **Section 5(a) — enactment-date language conflicts with the effective date.** It purports to cover violations “on or after the date of enactment,” while section 8 says the Act does not take effect for 180 days. Conduct during that interval is either not a violation at all or is subject to an unclear retroactive penalty.

44. **Section 5(b) — criminal “willfully” is undefined.** Courts use different meanings of “willfully,” including whether the defendant must know the conduct is unlawful. Combined with the Act’s vague technical standards, this may make prosecution unusually difficult or produce fair-notice challenges.

45. **Section 5(b) — responsibility inside corporations is unclear.** The bill does not specify liability for officers, directors, engineers, facility operators, or controlling persons who authorize or knowingly permit corporate violations. Nor does it provide a clear compliance defense or allocation of duties, leaving both evasion and arbitrary-enforcement concerns.

46. **Section 5 — no protection for whistleblowers.** Employees and contractors who disclose concealed training receive no anti-retaliation protection, reward, or secure reporting channel. Detection will therefore depend heavily on companies that have strong incentives not to report violations.

47. **Section 6 — international-negotiation duty is toothless.** “Shall seek to negotiate” requires only an effort and provides no substantive negotiating objectives beyond vague “equivalent” prohibitions, reporting obligation, consequence for delay, or enforcement mechanism. The 18-month language can be satisfied without obtaining an agreement.

48. **Section 6 — no interim controls on foreign enablement.** The Act does not restrict exports of chips, weights, technical assistance, cloud compute, financing, or U.S.-origin inputs while negotiations proceed. Foreign affiliates and partners could continue superintelligence development using U.S. resources.

49. **Section 7(a) — relationship to the sunset is contradictory.** It says the prohibition remains in effect until Congress makes a safety finding, but section 7(b) terminates the entire Act after 10 years regardless of any finding. The unconditional sunset therefore overrides the ostensible safety-based duration.

50. **Section 7(a) — National Academies process is incomplete.** The Academies are not actually directed or funded to produce a report, and there is no deadline, required content, evidentiary standard, conflict-of-interest rule, or definition of “safely.” Congress could therefore lack the contemplated report, or rely on one that does not answer the relevant question.

51. **Section 7(a) — safety finding is overbroad and underspecified.** A finding that covered systems “can be developed safely” does not require proof that enforceable safeguards exist, that deployment is safe, or that a particular risk level has been met. It is also unclear whether the joint resolution ends the prohibition automatically or must amend the Act.

52. **Section 7(b) — sunset terminates enforcement and oversight as well as the prohibition.** Because the entire Act “shall cease to have effect,” the registry, reporting system, international mandate, and possibly authority to pursue earlier violations all disappear. The bill does not preserve accrued liabilities, pending proceedings, records, or regulations.

53. **Section 8 — no transition rules.** The 180-day delay gives companies time to start nominal training runs and claim the section 3(b) exemption, move assets abroad, split facilities, or reorganize through foreign entities. There is no interim notification, standstill, or anti-evasion provision.

54. **Act-wide — no express rulemaking authority.** The responsible agencies are not clearly empowered or required to define technical terms, update thresholds, prescribe reports, establish evaluation protocols, or close newly discovered circumvention methods. Trying to implement those details without delegated authority would invite legal challenges.

55. **Act-wide — no appropriations, staffing, or implementation deadlines.** No funds or resources are authorized for capability evaluations, registry administration, inspections, investigations, or enforcement. The prohibition could consequently exist on paper without operational capacity.

56. **Act-wide — no information-sharing or confidentiality regime.** The bill neither authorizes Commerce, law-enforcement, intelligence, export-control, and energy agencies to share relevant information nor protects submitted trade secrets and security-sensitive model details. This may impair enforcement while making reporting requirements vulnerable to industry objections.

57. **Act-wide — no severability clause.** If a court invalidates a central definition, exemption, extraterritorial application, or delegation, it may have greater latitude to disturb the remaining statutory scheme. An express severability provision would reduce that risk.

58. **Act-wide — no treatment of government development or contractors.** The term “person” is undefined, and the bill does not clearly state whether federal agencies, government laboratories, federally funded research centers, or contractors acting for the government are covered. Defendants may invoke sovereign-status or procurement-related arguments, while agencies may assume they are exempt.

59. **Act-wide — no express preemption or savings rule.** The Act does not say whether stricter state AI laws remain valid or whether federal regulation occupies the field. Litigation over implied preemption could delay complementary state enforcement.

60. **Act-wide — no compliance duties before the threshold is crossed.** Developers need not estimate compute, notify the government of planned runs, implement access controls, preserve logs, or demonstrate that a run will remain below the threshold. Enforcement begins only after prohibited development may already have produced an uncontrollable or easily copied system.
